identity.title: How much can language models memorize?

problem.claim: Estimate how much language models know about individual datapoints and measure their memorization capacity.

gap.claim: Prior work has struggled to distinguish memorization from generalization.

contributions.claim: A method for estimating a model’s knowledge about a datapoint.
A formal decomposition of memorization into unintended memorization of a specific dataset and generalization about the true data-generating process.
Scaling laws connecting model capacity and data size to membership inference, based on hundreds of transformer models.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors’ stated distinction is the formal separation of memorization into unintended memorization and generalization, enabling total memorization estimates when generalization is eliminated.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report an estimated capacity of approximately 3.6 bits per parameter for GPT-style models when generalization is completely eliminated.
The authors report that models memorize as training datasets grow until capacity fills; afterward, unintended memorization decreases as models begin to generalize.
The authors report training hundreds of transformer language models spanning 500K to 1.5B parameters and deriving scaling laws relating capacity and data size to membership inference.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper frames the difficulty of separating memorization from generalization in prior studies.
It formally divides memorization into unintended dataset-specific information and generalization about the data-generating process.
Under complete elimination of generalization, it uses total memorization to estimate capacity at about 3.6 bits per parameter for GPT-style models.
Experiments varying dataset size report saturation of memorization followed by reduced unintended memorization, alongside scaling laws tied to membership inference.

source_observation.claim: The abstract defines distinct information targets before reporting capacity and scaling results: dataset-specific information, process-level information, and their separation.

lessons.interpretation: Separating confounded quantities can make a capacity claim more interpretable.
lessons.application: Define and operationalize the distinct components of a target phenomenon before presenting aggregate measurements.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the components cannot be independently defined or estimated from the available setup.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the proposed estimator, how generalization is completely eliminated, or how the 3.6-bits-per-parameter estimate is calculated.
The scaling-law forms, datasets, training procedures, and membership-inference evaluation details are not provided.
